t: Shell basics: pipes, redirection, exit codes
one: The shell runs programs and wires them together. Small tools chained with pipes answer questions about logs and files in seconds.
an: A kitchen assembly line: one station washes, the next chops, the next fries. Each does one thing; the conveyor belt (pipe) moves the food along.
how: cmd1 | cmd2 sends stdout of one to stdin of the next. > writes to a file, >> appends, 2>&1 merges errors into output.
Every command returns an exit code: 0 = success, anything else = failure. && runs the next only on success; || only on failure. CI and Docker rely on this.
Core tools: grep, sed, awk, sort, uniq -c, head/tail -f, wc -l, find, xargs, jq for JSON.
Scripts should start with set -euo pipefail so they stop on the first error.
why: Servers, containers, CI runners and incident debugging all happen in a shell. "Which IP sent the most 500s in the last hour?" is one line.
trade: Shell scripts grow fragile past ~50 lines. Move complex logic to a real language.

myth.m: The terminal is only for backend people.
myth.r: Every frontend build, deploy and CI pipeline is shell commands. Reading them fluently is part of owning your stack.

q.s: A CI step runs: npm test | tee results.txt. Tests fail but the step passes. Why?
o: tee hides output
The pipeline's exit code is tee's (0) unless pipefail is set
npm ignores failures
CI bug
q.e: Without set -o pipefail, a pipeline returns the last command's exit code.

Use jq to pull every error message out of a JSON log file and count them by type.

plain:
The shell is the program in your terminal that runs commands. Its superpower is connecting small tools: the output of one becomes the input of the next with a pipe |.

Every command also ends with an exit code. 0 means success; anything else means failure. Scripts, CI pipelines and Docker all decide what to do next based on that number.
bridge: npm run build && npm run deploy already uses this: && means “only deploy if build exited with 0”. Your CI pipeline turns red because some command exited with a non-zero code.

walk.title: Which IP sent the most failed requests today?
steps: Start with the log file: cat access.log. Thousands of lines, too many to read.
Keep only failures: grep ' 500 ' access.log.
Take only the IP column (the first word): | awk '{print $1}'.
Count each IP: | sort | uniq -c.
Show the top 5: | sort -rn | head -5. One line, a few seconds, and you know who to block or investigate.

terms: Sends one command's output into the next command's input.
Writes output into a file instead of the screen.
A number a command returns: 0 = success, other = failure.
The two output streams: normal output and error output.
insights: | pipes only stdout. To search error output too, merge it first: npm run build 2>&1 | grep -i error.
jq is the most useful tool for a web developer: it filters and reshapes JSON from APIs and logs, for example jq -r 'select(.level=="error") | .msg' app.log.
When a CI step fails, read the exit code before the log: 127 usually means a tool is missing from the CI image or PATH, not a bug in your code.

prod.summary: In production the shell is the glue in deploy scripts, CI steps, Docker entrypoints and incident one-liners. Seniors care less about clever pipes and more about scripts that fail loudly, quote every variable and return the right exit code, because CI and orchestrators trust that number completely.
checklist: Every bash script starts with #!/usr/bin/env bash and set -euo pipefail, and is checked by shellcheck in CI.
Every variable is quoted: "$file", not $file. A path with a space or an empty variable must not turn into a different command (think rm -rf "$DIR"/ with DIR empty).
Temporary files are created with mktemp and removed in a trap '...' EXIT, so a failed run leaves nothing behind.
The script exits non-zero on failure. Never end a CI step with || true unless you can explain exactly which failure is safe to ignore.
Docker entrypoint scripts end with exec "$@" so the real app replaces the shell and receives signals.
Anything over about 50 lines, with real data structures or retries, is rewritten in TypeScript or Python.
numbers: Exit code 0 = success; 126 = found but not executable; 127 = command not found; 128+N = killed by signal N (137 = SIGKILL, 143 = SIGTERM) — bash convention.
set -e is ignored inside if conditions, on the left of &&/||, and after ! — documented in the bash manual under set.
local x=$(cmd) always returns 0 (the status of local), so a failing cmd is hidden even with set -e; declare and assign on separate lines.
failures: CI step is green, but the test report shows failures. The step was npm test | tee out.txt.
A pipeline returns the exit code of its last command (tee, which succeeded). Add set -o pipefail so any failing stage fails the pipeline.
A cleanup script deleted far more than expected: it ran rm -rf $BUILD_DIR/*.
BUILD_DIR was empty, so the command became rm -rf /*. Use set -u (unset variable = error) and "${BUILD_DIR:?}", which aborts if it is empty.
Script works on your Mac but fails in CI with sed: -e expression #1: unknown command or wrong date output.
macOS ships BSD tools, CI runs GNU tools; sed -i, date -d and grep -P differ. Test in the same image as CI, or avoid non-portable flags.
A loop over files breaks on names with spaces: for f in $(ls *.log).
Word splitting cuts names at spaces. Use a glob directly: for f in *.log; do ... "$f"; done, or find ... -print0 | xargs -0.

code.title: A deploy script that fails safely
code.src:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail          # stop on error, unset var, failed pipe stage

APP_DIR="${APP_DIR:?APP_DIR must be set}"
TMP="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT    # always clean up, even on failure

log() { printf '%s %s\n' "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "$*" >&2; }

log "building"
npm ci --prefix "$APP_DIR"
npm run build --prefix "$APP_DIR" 2>&1 | tee "$TMP/build.log"

if ! curl -fsS --max-time 5 http://localhost:3000/health > /dev/null; then
  log "health check failed"
  exit 1
fi
log "deploy ok"
code.note: ${APP_DIR:?…} aborts on an empty variable, and pipefail makes the tee line fail when the build fails. curl -f turns HTTP 4xx/5xx into a non-zero exit code.

qs.s: A Docker entrypoint script does some setup and then runs node server.js as its last line (no exec). Deploys always wait the full 10 s before the container stops. What is the minimal fix?
o: Change the last line to exec node server.js
Add set -euo pipefail to the script
Increase the stop timeout to 30 s
Run node server.js & in the background
qs.e: Without exec, bash stays as PID 1 and does not forward SIGTERM to Node, so Docker kills it after 10 s. exec replaces the shell with Node, which then gets the signal. pipefail is good practice but unrelated to signals.

qs.s: This line is in a bash script with set -e: local token=$(curl -fsS https://auth/token). The auth server returns 500. What happens?
o: The script stops, because curl exited non-zero
The script stops, because -f makes curl print an error
The script continues with an empty token, because the line's exit code is that of local (0)
bash refuses to run the script
qs.e: The exit status of local x=$(...) is the status of local, which succeeds. Write local token on one line and token=$(curl ...) on the next so set -e can see the failure.

qs.s: In an incident you need the 5 paths with the most 5xx responses from an nginx access log where field 9 is the status and field 7 is the path. Which pipeline is correct?
o: grep 5 access.log | sort | uniq -c | head -5
awk '$9 ~ /^5/' access.log | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
awk '{print $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | head -5
awk '$9 ~ /^5/ {print $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
qs.e: You must filter by status, extract the path, sort before uniq -c (uniq only merges adjacent lines), then sort the counts numerically in reverse. The awk '$9 ~ /^5/' access.log | uniq -c answer skips the first sort and counts whole lines; the grep 5 answer matches any “5” anywhere in the line.

qs.s: Read this monitoring script. app.log exists but today it has no lines containing ERROR. What happens when it runs?

code.title: check-errors.sh
code.src:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

count=$(grep -c ERROR app.log)
echo "errors: $count"

if [ "$count" -gt 100 ]; then
  ./send-alert.sh "$count errors"
fi

o: It prints “errors: 0” and exits 0
It exits with code 1 on the count= line and prints nothing, because grep exits 1 when nothing matches and set -e stops the script
count is empty, so the [ ... -gt 100 ] test prints “integer expression expected”
pipefail makes the echo line fail
qs.e: grep exits 0 on a match, 1 on no match, 2 on an error. grep -c still prints 0, but the assignment takes grep's exit status (1), and set -e stops the script silently. Here “no match” is a normal result, so count=$(grep -c ERROR app.log || true) is a justified ignore. Many people expect A because the count is printed, but set -e acts on the exit status, not on the output.

qs.s: What does this bash session print? (Run line by line in one shell.)

code.title: terminal
code.src:
false | true; echo "status=$?"
set -o pipefail
false | true; echo "status=$?"
true | false | true; echo "pipe=${PIPESTATUS[*]}"

o: status=1, status=1, pipe=1
status=0, status=0, pipe=0 1 0
status=0, status=1, pipe=0 1 0
status=0, status=1, pipe=1
qs.e: Without pipefail a pipeline returns the last command's status (true = 0). With pipefail it returns the last non-zero status, so 1. PIPESTATUS is an array with the status of every stage of the last pipeline: 0 1 0. It is expanded before echo runs, so it still describes the pipeline. The answer with status=0 twice forgets that pipefail changes the second result.

qs.s: A nightly job runs find /var/app/tmp -name '*.tmp' -mtime +7 | xargs rm. It fails with “rm: cannot remove '/var/app/tmp/report': No such file or directory” because one file is called report final.tmp. Which fix is correct?
o: find /var/app/tmp -name '*.tmp' -mtime +7 -print0 | xargs -0 rm --, or simply find ... -delete
find ... | xargs "rm" — quoting the command fixes the names
Add set -euo pipefail so the error stops the job
for f in $(find /var/app/tmp -name '*.tmp' -mtime +7); do rm "$f"; done
qs.e: xargs splits its input on spaces and newlines by default. -print0 / -0 use a NUL byte as the separator, which can never appear in a file name. The for f in $(find ...) loop looks safe because "$f" is quoted, but $(find ...) is already split at the space before the loop sees it. pipefail only makes the failure louder.

qs.s: A setup script (no set -u) writes an nginx config with a here-doc. After deploy, nginx sends Host: with an empty value. Why?

code.title: write-nginx.sh

o: nginx does not support $host inside location
cat > drops lines that contain a dollar sign
The file needs chmod 644 before nginx can read the variable
With an unquoted EOF the shell expands $host itself (an empty shell variable). Use <<'EOF' so the text is written literally
qs.e: An unquoted here-doc delimiter means bash does variable and command expansion inside the body. $host is not a shell variable, so it becomes empty. Quoting the delimiter (<<'EOF') turns expansion off. With set -u the script would have stopped with “host: unbound variable” — one more reason to use it.

interview.q: You are reviewing a bash deploy script that runs in CI. What do you check to make it safe?
answer: Strict mode: set -euo pipefail, and knowing its holes: set -e is ignored in if conditions and &&/|| lists, and local x=$(cmd) hides the failure.
Every variable quoted; required variables guarded with "${VAR:?message}", especially anything near rm -rf.
Cleanup with mktemp + trap ... EXIT; the script can be re-run safely after a half-failed run (idempotent).
Timeouts on every network call (curl --max-time, -f so HTTP errors become exit codes) and a health check before reporting success.
shellcheck in CI; logs go to stderr with timestamps; secrets are never echoed (set -x prints them).
Know when to stop: past ~50 lines, retries or JSON handling, move it to TypeScript or Python.
followups: What does set -e NOT catch?
How would you test this script before it runs against production?

interview.q: There is no log platform. You have 2 GB of JSON logs on one server. How do you find which endpoint started returning 500s after 14:00?
answer: Look at a few lines first (head -3 app.log | jq .) to learn the field names.
Filter early and cheaply: narrow by time first, then by status, then extract one field: jq -r 'select(.time >= "2026-10-03T14:00" and .status >= 500) | .path' then sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head.
Compare with the hour before 14:00 to see what is new, not only what is large.
Include rotated files with zcat/zgrep; a grep prefilter before jq is much faster on big files.
Be careful on a production box: run with nice/ionice, or copy the file elsewhere, so the analysis does not slow the app.
followups: Why must sort come before uniq -c?
How would you get the p95 latency per path from the same file?

interview.q: What is the difference between stdout and stderr, and why does it matter for containers and CI?
answer: Two separate streams: file descriptor 1 (stdout) for results, 2 (stderr) for diagnostics. A pipe only carries stdout.
Keep machine-readable output on stdout and logs on stderr, so tool | jq works even when the tool logs.
Order of redirects matters: cmd >out.txt 2>&1 sends both to the file; cmd 2>&1 >out.txt sends stderr to the terminal.
Containers: the runtime captures both streams as logs; write logs there, not to files inside the container.
Buffering: stdout is often block-buffered when it is not a terminal, so logs may appear late or be lost on a crash (for example Python needs PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1).
followups: Why does cmd | tee log sometimes hide errors in CI?
How do you send only stderr through a pipe?

one: Every running program is a process with an ID. Signals like SIGTERM and SIGKILL ask it to stop, and handling SIGTERM properly is what makes deploys lose zero requests.
an: SIGTERM is closing time: "please finish serving and leave". SIGKILL is the power being cut.
how: ps aux, top/htop list processes. kill PID sends SIGTERM; kill -9 sends SIGKILL, which cannot be caught or delayed.
Docker sends SIGTERM and waits 10 s by default (docker stop -t); Kubernetes runs the preStop hook, sends SIGTERM, and SIGKILLs when terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30 s) runs out.

Graceful shutdown: on SIGTERM, stop taking new work, finish in-flight requests and jobs, close DB pools, and exit 0. On Kubernetes, the pod is removed from the load balancer at the same time as shutdown starts, not before, so the app must keep serving for a few seconds first (a preStop sleep).

PID 1 in containers: the kernel does not apply default signal actions to PID 1, so a Node process with no SIGTERM handler simply ignores it. And if PID 1 is sh -c or npm start, the signal may never reach Node. Use exec-form CMD ["node", "server.js"], handle SIGTERM in code, or add an init (docker run --init / tini).
why: Dropped requests and half-processed jobs on every deploy are almost always a shutdown-handling bug.
trade: Long grace periods slow deploys; short ones kill work. Size it to your longest normal request or job chunk.

myth.r: They are asked politely first. Whether your app listens decides whether users see errors during deploys.

q.s: Every deploy, some requests fail and docker stop always takes exactly 10 seconds. The Dockerfile uses CMD npm start. Likely cause?
o: Too few replicas
SIGTERM never reaches a handler in Node (npm in front of it, or no handler at all), so it is SIGKILLed at the 10 s timeout
DNS caching
CORS
q.e: Exactly 10 s is Docker's default stop timeout, so the process ignored SIGTERM. Run node directly with exec-form CMD and add a SIGTERM handler; as PID 1, Node without a handler ignores SIGTERM.

lab: Write a Node server that logs on SIGTERM, stops accepting connections with server.close(), waits for in-flight requests, then exits.
Run it in Docker with CMD npm start, time docker stop, then switch to exec form and time again.

plain:
Every running program is a process with a number (PID). The system talks to processes using signals. The two that matter most: SIGTERM means “please stop, clean up first”. SIGKILL means “stop now”, and the program cannot refuse or clean up.

When you deploy, the platform sends SIGTERM to the old version, waits a few seconds, then sends SIGKILL. If your app ignores SIGTERM, every deploy cuts off users in the middle of requests.
bridge: Pressing Ctrl+C in your terminal sends SIGINT, a similar polite stop. When your Vite dev server prints a goodbye message and exits cleanly, it handled that signal.

walk.title: A zero-error deploy on Kubernetes, step by step
steps: Kubernetes starts the new pod and waits until its readiness probe passes.
It begins deleting the old pod. Two things now happen in parallel: the pod is removed from the Service endpoints, and the kubelet runs preStop and then sends SIGTERM.
Endpoint removal takes a few seconds to reach every node and ingress. A preStop sleep of about 5 s keeps the old pod serving the requests that still arrive during that time.
Your SIGTERM handler calls server.close(): no new connections, in-flight requests (for example, a 2-second upload) finish, the DB pool closes, the process exits 0.
If the app ignored SIGTERM, Kubernetes would SIGKILL it when the 30 s grace period ends, cutting off whatever was in progress.

terms: A running program and its ID number.
A short message from the OS to a process, like SIGTERM or SIGKILL.
Stopping new work, finishing current work, then exiting.
The first process in a container. It must forward signals or the app never sees them.
insights: Test shutdown instead of assuming it works: time docker stop. If it takes exactly 10 seconds, your app ignored SIGTERM and was SIGKILLed.
Background job workers need graceful shutdown even more than web servers, or jobs die half-done on every deploy.
Ctrl+C sends SIGINT, platforms send SIGTERM. A handler for only one of them means local tests pass while production deploys still cut requests.

prod.summary: In production, processes are started and stopped by an orchestrator (Docker, Kubernetes, systemd) dozens of times a day. Seniors check that SIGTERM reaches the app, that the app drains instead of dying, and that the grace period is longer than the slowest normal request or job step.
checklist: The container's PID 1 is the app itself (exec-form CMD) or a real init (--init, tini, dumb-init), never a shell wrapper without exec.
The app has a SIGTERM handler that stops accepting work, drains, closes pools and exits with 0; it also has a hard timeout so it cannot hang forever.
On Kubernetes, a preStop sleep (native sleep action, GA in 1.34) of 5–10 s covers the endpoint-removal race.
terminationGracePeriodSeconds is larger than preStop sleep + the longest request or job chunk.
Queue workers stop pulling new jobs on SIGTERM and either finish or release (re-queue) the current job.
Dashboards show container exit codes: a stream of 137s means SIGKILL (OOM or timeout), not graceful exits.
numbers: Docker docker stop default timeout: 10 s before SIGKILL.
Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds default: 30 s, and it includes the time spent in preStop.
systemd DefaultTimeoutStopSec: 90 s before it escalates to SIGKILL.
Exit code 143 = 128 + 15 (SIGTERM), 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL).
failures: 502/503 spikes for 1–3 seconds during every rolling deploy, even though the app handles SIGTERM.
The app closes its listener immediately on SIGTERM, but ingress and kube-proxy still route to it for a few seconds. Add a preStop sleep (5–10 s) and only then close the server.
Pods show Exit Code: 137 and Reason: Error (not OOMKilled) after every rollout.

The process outlived the grace period and was SIGKILLed: usually long-polling or keep-alive connections that never close. Close idle connections on shutdown (Node 19+ server.close() does this) and add a hard exit timer.
Background jobs are processed twice, or left half-done, after deploys.
The worker was killed mid-job. Stop fetching on SIGTERM, finish or release the current job, and make jobs idempotent because a SIGKILL can always happen.
Zombie processes (<defunct> in ps) pile up in a container that spawns child processes (Chrome, ffmpeg).
PID 1 is your app, which does not reap orphaned children. Run with --init or tini as PID 1.

code.title: Graceful shutdown for a Node HTTP server
code.note: The DB pool is closed only inside the server.close callback, after in-flight requests finish. Since Node 19, server.close() also closes idle keep-alive connections. The hard-stop timer (25 s) fits Kubernetes' 30 s grace period only without a preStop hook. The grace period includes preStop, so with a 5 s preStop sleep SIGTERM arrives at 5 s and the timer would fire at 30 s, exactly when the kubelet sends SIGKILL. Keep preStop + timer below the grace period: lower the timer (for example 20 s) or raise terminationGracePeriodSeconds.

qs.s: Your pod spec has preStop sleep 20 s and terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30. The slowest normal request takes 15 s. What happens to a 15 s request that starts right when SIGTERM arrives?
o: It completes; SIGTERM only arrives after preStop, and 30 s is plenty
It completes, because SIGKILL is never sent while requests are open
It may be cut off: preStop uses 20 s of the 30 s budget, leaving only 10 s after SIGTERM
It is cut off immediately, because SIGTERM closes all sockets
qs.e: The grace period counts from the start of termination and includes preStop. 30 − 20 = 10 s remain after SIGTERM, less than 15 s. Raise the grace period or shorten the sleep.

qs.s: A container runs CMD ["node", "server.js"]. The code has no signal handlers. docker stop takes 10 s every time. Why, if there is no npm or shell in front?
o: Node is PID 1, and the kernel does not apply the default “terminate” action to PID 1, so SIGTERM is ignored without a handler
Exec form never forwards signals
Docker sends SIGINT, which Node ignores
Node always waits 10 s for open sockets
qs.e: PID 1 in a namespace only reacts to signals it has handlers for. Add process.on("SIGTERM", ...) or run with --init, which forwards the signal to a non-PID-1 Node that then exits by default.

qs.s: A queue worker pulls a job, then spends up to 2 minutes on it. Deploys use Kubernetes defaults. Which change makes deploys safe for this worker?
o: Add a readiness probe
On SIGTERM stop pulling jobs, finish or re-queue the current one, and raise terminationGracePeriodSeconds above 2 minutes (or split jobs into shorter steps)
Switch to kill -9 for faster deploys
Set restartPolicy: Never
qs.e: The default 30 s grace is shorter than the job. Readiness only affects HTTP traffic, not queue pulling. Either give the worker enough time or make jobs short and resumable.

qs.s: Read this shutdown handler. A deploy sends SIGTERM while 20 requests are in progress, and each of them still needs one more DB query. What happens?

code.title: shutdown.ts

o: Nothing is lost: server.close() waits for in-flight requests before the process exits
Node does not allow an async signal handler, so SIGTERM is ignored
Those requests fail: the pool is closed while they still need it, and process.exit(0) runs right away, without waiting for server.close() to finish
pool.end() hangs forever, because I/O is blocked during a signal
qs.e: Two bugs. First, the pool is ended before the requests are done, so their next query throws (pg: “Cannot use a pool after calling end on the pool”). Second, server.close() is asynchronous: it only stops new connections and calls its callback later, but process.exit(0) runs on the next line and kills everything. “server.close() waits for in-flight requests” is the tempting answer; it is only true if you exit inside the close callback.

qs.s: A pod restarted 4 times today. Read the output. What happened?

code.title: kubectl describe pod api-7c9f
code.src:
State:          Running
Last State:     Terminated
  Reason:       Error
  Exit Code:    143
Restart Count:  4
Liveness:   http-get http://:3000/healthz delay=0s timeout=1s period=10s #success=1 #failure=3
Events:
  Warning  Unhealthy  kubelet  Liveness probe failed: Get "http://10.1.2.3:3000/healthz": context deadline exceeded
  Normal   Killing    kubelet  Container api failed liveness probe, will be restarted

o: The liveness probe timed out (1 s limit) 3 times in a row, so the kubelet sent SIGTERM and restarted the container; 143 means it exited on SIGTERM. Find out why /healthz is slow (blocked event loop, a probe that calls the DB)
The container ran out of memory; 143 is the OOM exit code
The app crashed with an uncaught exception; Node exits with 143 in that case
The app ignored SIGTERM and was SIGKILLed at the end of the grace period
qs.e: 143 = 128 + 15 (SIGTERM): the process stopped because it was asked to. The events say why: the liveness probe failed. An uncaught exception exits with 1, OOM and an ignored SIGTERM end with 137 (SIGKILL). A liveness probe with a 1 s timeout on a busy Node process is a classic cause of restart loops under load.

qs.s: A worker handles process.on("SIGINT", shutdown). Ctrl+C on a laptop shuts it down cleanly. In Docker, docker stop takes 10 s every time and jobs are cut off. The Dockerfile uses exec-form CMD. Why?
o: Docker sends SIGKILL, never SIGINT
Exec-form CMD blocks all signals
Docker waits 10 s by design before it sends any signal
docker stop sends SIGTERM (unless STOPSIGNAL says otherwise). The app only handles SIGINT, and as PID 1 it ignores unhandled signals, so it is SIGKILLed after 10 s. Handle SIGTERM too
qs.e: Ctrl+C sends SIGINT; orchestrators send SIGTERM. Register the same handler for both. “Docker sends SIGKILL, never SIGINT” is half true: SIGKILL does come, but only after the 10 s timeout, because the first signal (SIGTERM) was ignored.

qs.s: The app's hard-exit timer fires 25 s after SIGTERM. Long-poll connections keep server.close() from finishing. Given this pod spec, which exit code do you see after a rollout?

code.title: deployment.yaml (excerpt)
code.src:
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: api:1.4
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          sleep:
            seconds: 10

o: 1, from the app's hard-exit timer
137: SIGTERM arrives at t=10 s, the timer would fire at t=35 s, but the kubelet sends SIGKILL at t=30 s
143, because the app received SIGTERM
0, because preStop finished successfully
qs.e: The grace period starts when deletion starts and includes preStop. SIGTERM only comes after the 10 s sleep, so the app's 25 s timer ends at 35 s, after the 30 s deadline. Keep preStop + app hard timeout below the grace period: here, a timer of about 15 s, or a grace period of about 45 s.

interview.q: Design graceful shutdown for a Node API running on Kubernetes behind an ingress. Users must see zero errors during deploys.
answer: Signals must reach Node: exec-form CMD ["node", "server.js"] or tini, and a SIGTERM handler (as PID 1, Node ignores SIGTERM without one).
Cover the endpoint-removal race: a preStop sleep of 5–10 s, because endpoints and ingress are updated in parallel with SIGTERM, not before it.
On SIGTERM: server.close(), let in-flight requests finish, then close DB pools and queue consumers, then exit 0. Long-lived connections (long-poll, WebSockets) need an explicit close.
A hard-exit timer so shutdown cannot hang, and terminationGracePeriodSeconds > preStop + longest request + timer margin.
Prove it: run a load test (k6) during kubectl rollout restart and require zero non-2xx responses.
followups: Why not just fail the readiness probe and skip the preStop sleep?
How does this change for WebSocket connections?

interview.q: Explain SIGTERM, SIGINT, SIGKILL and SIGHUP. Which can a process catch, and how do you tell from an exit code what happened?
answer: SIGTERM (15): the polite stop sent by Docker, Kubernetes and systemd; catchable.
SIGINT (2): Ctrl+C in a terminal; catchable. SIGHUP (1): terminal hang-up, often used to mean “reload config” (nginx, many daemons).
SIGKILL (9) and SIGSTOP cannot be caught, blocked or ignored; there is no cleanup.
A process killed by signal N reports exit code 128+N in shells and containers: 143 = SIGTERM, 137 = SIGKILL (often OOM or a grace-period timeout), 130 = SIGINT.
PID 1 in a container is special: the kernel ignores signals for which it has no handler.
followups: Exit code 137 but Reason is not OOMKilled — what else could it be?
What signal does nginx use to reopen log files?

interview.q: A container that runs headless Chrome slowly fills with zombie processes and finally fails with “fork: Resource temporarily unavailable”. What is going on?
answer: A zombie is a child that has exited but whose parent has not called wait() to collect its exit status. It uses almost no memory but keeps its PID.
Orphaned grandchildren are re-parented to PID 1. If PID 1 is your app, it never reaps them.
PIDs are limited (the container's pids.max cgroup limit or the kernel's pid_max), so eventually fork() fails.
Fix: run a real init as PID 1 (docker run --init, tini, dumb-init), and make sure the app waits for the child processes it starts.
Check with ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,cmd: state Z and <defunct>.
followups: Can you kill a zombie with kill -9?
How does Kubernetes' shareProcessNamespace change who reaps?

one: Linux decides access by user, group and permission bits on each file. Running everything as root is the fastest way to turn a bug into a breach.
an: Every room has three locks: one for the owner, one for their team, one for everyone else, each allowing read, write or enter.
how: ls -l shows -rwxr-x---: owner can read/write/execute, group can read/execute, others nothing. Numeric: 750.
chmod changes bits, chown changes owner. Directories need x to be entered.
sudo runs one command as root. Services and containers should run as an unprivileged user.
Private keys must be readable only by you (chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519) or SSH refuses them.
why: Permission errors in containers, volumes and deploy scripts are daily debugging. Least privilege on the OS is part of security.
trade: chmod 777 "fixes" permission errors by making everything writable by everyone. It is never the right fix.

myth.m: Inside a container, root is harmless.
myth.r: Container root maps to host root unless user namespaces are used. A container escape as root is far worse.

q.s: A containerised app cannot write to a mounted volume: permission denied. Which fix is right?
o: chmod -R 777 the volume
Match the volume's ownership to the container's non-root UID (or set fsGroup in Kubernetes)
Run the container as root
Disable the volume
q.e: Fix ownership for the specific user, keep the app unprivileged.

more: UIDs/GIDs and how containers map them
lab: Create a user, a group, and a directory only that group can write to. Test access as each user.
Run docker run --user 1000:1000 with a bind mount and fix the resulting permission error properly.
docs: Arch Wiki: File permissions and attributes

plain:
Linux gives every file an owner, a group, and three sets of rights: what the owner can do, what the group can do, what everyone else can do. Each set is read, write and execute.

The root user can do anything. Programs should not run as root, so that a bug or attack in the program cannot damage the whole system.
bridge: The macOS “permission denied” you get when running a script you just downloaded is this system: the file has no execute right. chmod +x script.sh adds it.

walk.title: Fixing “permission denied” in a container the right way
steps: Your app container runs as user 1000 (not root), which is good practice.
It writes uploads to a mounted folder /data, and crashes with “EACCES: permission denied”.
ls -ln /data shows the folder belongs to user 0 (root) with rights drwxr-xr-x: only root can write.
Wrong fix: chmod 777 /data (everyone can write everything).
Right fix: chown 1000:1000 /data (or fsGroup in Kubernetes), so exactly your app's user can write.

terms: Changes the rights on a file.
insights: Use ls -ln (numeric IDs) when debugging containers. User names can differ between the image and the host; the UID numbers are what the kernel compares.
Creating or deleting a file needs w on the directory, not on the file. That is why a read-only file can still be deleted from a writable folder.
Running containers as non-root is one of the cheapest security wins available.

prod.summary: In production, permissions show up as containers running as root, volumes the app cannot write, and secrets readable by the wrong user. Seniors make the app run as a fixed non-root UID, give it write access only where it needs it, and treat chmod 777 or privileged: true in a review as a blocker.
checklist: The image sets a non-root USER (the official Node image has node, UID 1000) and Kubernetes sets runAsNonRoot: true.
Files copied into the image are owned by root and read-only for the app (COPY default); only specific data directories are writable by the app user.
Volumes are owned by the app's UID, or Kubernetes fsGroup sets group ownership, instead of chmod 777.
Secrets and keys on disk are 600 or 400 and owned by the service user; .env files are never world-readable.
Containers drop capabilities (capabilities: drop: ["ALL"]), set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false and, where possible, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true.
No user or CI runner is in the docker group or mounts /var/run/docker.sock without a reason: that access equals root on the host.
sudo on servers is per person and logged, not one shared admin account.
numbers: With umask 022 (the usual default for root, system services and containers; systemd's UMask= default is 0022), new files get 644 and new directories 755. Many distros give normal login users 002 instead.
OpenSSH refuses a private key that others can read: “Permissions 0644 for '...' are too open” — use 600.

On a host, ports below 1024 need root or CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE (ip_unprivileged_port_start defaults to 1024). Docker 20.10+ sets it to 0 inside containers, so this bites mainly systemd services on VMs.
UID 0 is root; inside a container without user namespaces, UID 0 is the same UID 0 as on the host.
failures: App logs EACCES: permission denied, open '/data/uploads/x.png' after switching the image to non-root.
The volume is owned by root from the old image. ls -ln /data to see the numeric owner, then chown 1000:1000 it, use an init step, or set fsGroup: 1000 in Kubernetes.
Error: listen EACCES: permission denied 0.0.0.0:80 after moving a VM service to User=api.
Non-root cannot bind ports below 1024 on the host. Listen on 3000/8080 behind nginx or Caddy, or grant only that right with AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE in the unit.
Files created by a bind-mounted dev container are owned by root on your laptop, and git cannot delete them.
The container ran as root and wrote with UID 0. Run it with --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)".
SSH login with a key suddenly fails; /var/log/auth.log says “Authentication refused: bad ownership or modes for directory /home/deploy”.
sshd's StrictModes rejects a home or .ssh directory that others can write. Set chmod 700 ~/.ssh, 600 authorized_keys, and remove group/world write from the home directory.
A user was added to a group with usermod -aG data app, but the service still gets “Permission denied” on the group's files.
Group membership is read when a process starts. Restart the service (or log in again for a shell); id in the old session still shows the old groups.

code.title: Non-root Node image with only one writable directory
code.src:
FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app

# app code stays owned by root: the app user can read it, not change it
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .

# the only place the app may write
RUN mkdir -p /app/data && chown node:node /app/data

# "node" is UID 1000 in the official image. Use the number:
# Kubernetes runAsNonRoot can only verify a numeric user.
# (comments must be on their own line: Dockerfiles have no inline comments)
USER 1000
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
code.note: If an attacker gets code execution, they cannot modify the app's own files, only /app/data. Using COPY --chown=node:node . . would make the whole app writable, which is weaker. With USER node (a name), a pod with runAsNonRoot: true fails with “image has non-numeric user (node), cannot verify user is non-root”; USER 1000 passes. Writing USER 1000 # comment on one line would make Docker use the literal user “1000 # comment”.

qs.s: ls -l deploy.sh shows -rw-r--r-- 1 ci ci. The CI job runs ./deploy.sh as user ci and gets “Permission denied”. Which fix is correct and minimal?
o: chmod 777 deploy.sh
chown root deploy.sh
chmod +x deploy.sh (or run it as bash deploy.sh) and commit the mode change
Run the job with sudo
qs.e: The file has no execute bit (rw-). Adding x is enough; git tracks the executable bit. 777 also makes it writable by everyone, which is the wrong fix.

qs.s: A directory has mode drwxr--r-- owned by app. User bob (not in the group) runs cat /dir/notes.txt, and the file itself is -rw-r--r--. What happens?
o: It works, because the file is world-readable
It works, because the directory is world-readable
It fails only if bob is not root
It fails, because bob has no x on the directory, so he cannot reach any file inside it
qs.e: To open a path you need x (search) on every directory in it. r on a directory only lets you list names. Readable files inside an unsearchable directory are still unreachable.

qs.s: A Kubernetes pod runs as UID 1000 with a new PersistentVolume and fails with EACCES on write. Which setting fixes it without running as root?
o: securityContext.fsGroup: 1000, so the volume is group-owned by GID 1000 and group-writable
privileged: true
runAsUser: 0 in an init container that then does chmod 777
readOnlyRootFilesystem: false
qs.e: fsGroup makes supported volumes owned by that group and writable by it. Privileged mode and root init containers with 777 work but throw away the isolation you wanted.

qs.s: Read the output. User app runs cat /srv/shared/report.csv. What happens, and what is the right fix?

code.title: terminal
code.src:
$ id
uid=1000(app) gid=1000(app) groups=1000(app)
$ ls -ld /srv/shared /srv/shared/report.csv
drwxrwx--- 2 root data 4096 Oct  3 10:00 /srv/shared
-rw-rw-r-- 1 root data  812 Oct  3 10:00 /srv/shared/report.csv

o: It works, because the file is readable by others (r--)
“Permission denied”; fix with chmod o+r report.csv
It works, because root owns both and root's rights apply
“Permission denied”, because app is not in data and others have no x on the directory. Fix: usermod -aG data app, then restart the service or log in again
qs.e: To open a file you need x on every directory in the path. For app, the directory falls into the “others” class (---), so the readable file inside does not matter. chmod o+r report.csv changes the wrong object: the file is already world-readable. New group membership only applies to processes started after the change.

qs.s: To let CI jobs build images, the runner user was added to the docker group. A security reviewer blocks this. Why?
o: The docker group can only pull images, so it is harmless; the reviewer is wrong
Membership in the docker group is equal to root on the host: any job can run docker run -v /:/host ... and change any host file
It is only a problem if containers use --privileged
It is only a problem because the group name is predictable
qs.e: The docker group can talk to the Docker daemon socket, and the daemon runs as root. Mounting the host's root filesystem into a container gives full control, no --privileged needed. Safer options: rootless Docker or Podman, or a daemonless builder (BuildKit rootless, Kaniko-style builders) on isolated runners.

qs.s: This pod is created. The image's Dockerfile has no USER line. What happens?

code.title: pod.yaml
code.src:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: myorg/api:2.1

o: The container does not start: status CreateContainerConfigError, “container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root”
It runs as root; runAsNonRoot only logs a warning
Kubernetes picks a random non-root UID and runs it
It runs as UID 65534 (nobody)
qs.e: runAsNonRoot is a check, not a change: the kubelet refuses to start a container whose user would be UID 0. Fix it by adding USER 1000 (numeric is best, so the kubelet can verify it) to the image or runAsUser: 1000 to the pod. Random UIDs are an OpenShift behaviour, not plain Kubernetes.

qs.s: What permissions do the new directory and file get?

code.title: terminal
code.src:
umask 027
mkdir logs
touch logs/a.log
ls -ld logs logs/a.log

o: drwxr-xr-x and -rw-r--r--
drwxrwxr-x and -rw-rw-r--
drwxr-x--- and -rw-r-----
drwxr-x--- and -rwxr-x---
qs.e: The umask removes bits from the default: directories start from 777, files from 666 (no execute). 777 − 027 = 750; 666 with 027 removed = 640. -rwxr-x--- forgets that new files never get execute bits by default. drwxr-xr-x / -rw-r--r-- is the result of umask 022, and drwxrwxr-x / -rw-rw-r-- of umask 002.

interview.q: How do you run a containerised service with least privilege, on Docker and on Kubernetes?
answer: A fixed, numeric non-root user in the image (USER 1000) and runAsNonRoot: true; app code owned by root and read-only.
readOnlyRootFilesystem: true with small writable mounts (emptyDir for /tmp, a volume for data).
Drop all capabilities and add back only what is needed (for example NET_BIND_SERVICE); allowPrivilegeEscalation: false stops setuid binaries from gaining rights.
Seccomp RuntimeDefault; no privileged, no hostPath, never mount the Docker socket. Enforce it cluster-wide with Pod Security Admission at the “restricted” level.
Where supported, user namespaces (hostUsers: false) so container root is not host root.
followups: Which of these breaks most apps when you turn it on, and how do you fix it?
Why prefer a numeric UID over a user name in the image?

interview.q: A process tries to open a file. Walk me through how Linux decides whether it is allowed.
answer: The kernel uses the process's effective UID, GID and supplementary groups (fixed when the process started).

It needs x on every directory in the path, then checks the file's bits for one class only: owner if the UID matches, else group if a group matches, else others. An owner with fewer rights than “others” is denied.
Root (or a process with CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE) skips most of these checks.
ACLs (getfacl) can add rules on top of the bits.
After that, SELinux or AppArmor can still deny. That explains “Permission denied” when ls -l looks correct; check ausearch/dmesg for AVC denials.
followups: What does the setuid bit do, and why is it dangerous?
Why does a directory need x and not only r?

interview.q: A bind-mounted volume works on your Mac but fails with EACCES on the Linux CI server. Why, and how do you fix it properly?
answer: On Linux, a bind mount shows the host's real numeric UIDs and GIDs; names do not matter, only numbers.
Docker Desktop on macOS shares files through a VM layer that maps ownership, so mismatches are hidden on laptops.
Diagnose with ls -ln on the host and id inside the container.
Fix by matching numbers: chown the directory to the container's UID, run with --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)", use fsGroup in Kubernetes, or use a named volume initialised from the image.
On RHEL/Fedora hosts, SELinux may also block it: mount with :z or :Z to relabel.
followups: Why is chmod 777 on the mount the wrong fix?
How do rootless containers change the UID mapping?

diagrams.title: How Linux decides: can UID 1000 create a file in /data?
diagrams.caption: What to notice: Linux uses only the first class that matches (owner, then group, then others). In the walkthrough, /data is drwxr-xr-x owned by root, so UID 1000 falls to “others” (r-x), has no w, and gets EACCES. chown 1000:1000 /data moves it to the owner branch.

one: SSH gives you an encrypted shell on a remote machine, authenticated with key pairs. It also tunnels ports and copies files.
an: Your private key is the physical key; the server's authorized_keys file is the list of locks that key opens.
how: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 creates a key pair. The public key goes into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server; the private key never leaves your machine.
~/.ssh/config stores host aliases, users, ports and which key to use per host.
Port forwarding: ssh -L 5433:localhost:5432 server lets you reach a server's private Postgres on your own port 5433, without exposing it publicly.
Harden servers: disable password login and root login, use keys only, keep packages updated, consider fail2ban.
why: Every VM deploy, debugging session and private database access goes through SSH.
trade: SSH keys without a passphrase on a stolen laptop are a skeleton key to your servers. Use passphrases with the agent, or hardware keys.

myth.m: Changing the SSH port makes the server secure.
myth.r: It reduces log noise. Key-only auth and disabled passwords are what actually protect it.

q.s: You need to inspect a production Postgres that only listens on the server's private interface. Safest quick access?
o: Open port 5432 to the internet temporarily
An SSH tunnel: ssh -L 5433:localhost:5432 server, then connect to localhost:5433
Email yourself a dump
Disable the firewall
q.e: The DB stays private; traffic goes through your authenticated, encrypted SSH session.

more: SSH agent and agent forwarding risks
lab: Create an ed25519 key with a passphrase, add it to the agent, and set up a ~/.ssh/config alias for a server.
On a $5 VM: disable password and root login in sshd_config, restart sshd, and confirm you can still log in with your key.
Open an SSH tunnel to a remote service and use it locally.
docs: GitHub: Generating a new SSH key

plain:
SSH lets you open a terminal on another computer over the internet, safely encrypted. You prove who you are with a key pair: a private key that never leaves your laptop, and a public key you put on the server.

SSH can also tunnel: it can make a port on the server appear on your laptop, so you can reach private things like a database without exposing them to the internet.
bridge: If you push to GitHub with a git@github.com:... URL, you already use SSH keys. The same key idea logs you into servers.

walk.title: Looking at a production database that is not public
steps: The database only listens on the server's internal address, port 5432. Good: the internet cannot reach it.
You run ssh -L 5433:localhost:5432 deploy@my-server.
SSH logs you in with your key and opens a tunnel: your laptop's port 5433 now leads to the server's port 5432.
You connect your database tool (TablePlus, DBeaver) to localhost:5433.
When you close the SSH session, the tunnel disappears. The database was never exposed.

terms: A private key (secret) and a public key (shareable) that work together.
The file on the server listing public keys allowed to log in.
Making a remote port reachable through the SSH connection.
Your file of shortcuts: host names, users, which key to use.
insights: Disable password login on every server you own; bots try passwords all day.
Put a passphrase on your private key and use the SSH agent so you type it once per session.
Tunnels are the safe way to reach admin tools and databases. Opening their ports to the internet “just for a minute” is how breaches happen.

prod.summary: In production, SSH is the door to every VM, bastion and private database, so it is a top target for bots. Seniors make it key-only, keep the keys protected and per person, reach private hosts through a bastion with ProxyJump, and make sure a change to sshd_config cannot lock everyone out.
checklist: PasswordAuthentication no and PermitRootLogin no (or prohibit-password) in sshd config; verify with sshd -T | grep -i -e password -e permitroot.
Keys are ed25519 (or FIDO2 ed25519-sk), have a passphrase, and are one per person, so access can be removed from authorized_keys when someone leaves.
Test config with sshd -t before reloading, and keep a second session open while you change sshd settings.
Private hosts are reached through a bastion with ProxyJump, not by copying private keys onto the bastion. Avoid ForwardAgent yes to shared hosts: root there can use your agent.
Host keys are verified (known_hosts); a “REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED” warning is investigated, not bypassed.
Port 22 is open only to the IPs that need it (security group / firewall), or SSH is replaced by a provider tool like AWS SSM Session Manager.
numbers: OpenSSH 10.0 (April 2025) removed DSA keys entirely and made the post-quantum hybrid mlkem768x25519-sha256 the default key exchange.
sshd default MaxAuthTries is 6: a client offering many agent keys can hit “Too many authentication failures” before trying the right one — set IdentitiesOnly yes.
sshd default LoginGraceTime is 120 s to finish authenticating.
failures: Received disconnect: Too many authentication failures when connecting to a new server.
Your agent offers every key it holds and sshd stops after MaxAuthTries. In ~/.ssh/config set IdentityFile for that host plus IdentitiesOnly yes.
After a hardening change, nobody can log in; the cloud console shows sshd failed to start.
A typo in sshd_config. Always run sshd -t before systemctl reload ssh and keep one session open. Recover through the provider's serial console.
WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED! after a server was rebuilt.
Expected after a rebuild (new host key): remove the old entry with ssh-keygen -R host. If nothing was rebuilt, stop — it could be a man-in-the-middle.
auth.log shows thousands of failed logins per hour from random IPs.
Normal internet noise against port 22. Harmless if passwords are disabled; restrict the port in the firewall or add fail2ban to cut the noise. Changing the port only hides it.

code.title: Client config with a bastion, and server hardening
code.src:
# ~/.ssh/config (your laptop)
# ssh_config has no end-of-line comments: keep # on its own line
Host bastion
  HostName bastion.example.com
  User deploy
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
  IdentitiesOnly yes

Host db-1
  # private IP, not reachable directly
  HostName 10.0.2.15
  User deploy
  # hop through the bastion; your key stays on your laptop
  ProxyJump bastion
  LocalForward 5433 localhost:5432

# /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hardening.conf (server)
PasswordAuthentication no
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin no
AllowUsers deploy
# then: sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload ssh
code.note: ssh db-1 now jumps through the bastion and opens the Postgres tunnel on localhost:5433. Comments go on their own line: ProxyJump bastion # hop makes ssh use “bastion # hop” as the jump host and the jump breaks. The service is called ssh on Debian/Ubuntu and sshd on RHEL/Fedora.

qs.s: You need to reach a server on a private subnet through a bastion. A teammate suggests copying your private key onto the bastion. What is the better option and why?
o: Copy the key but chmod 600 it
Use ProxyJump bastion: the bastion only forwards an encrypted connection, and your key never leaves your laptop
Enable ForwardAgent yes on the bastion, which is always safe
Open the private server's port 22 to the internet
qs.e: With ProxyJump, authentication to the target happens end to end from your laptop. A key copied to the bastion is stolen if the bastion is. Agent forwarding lets root on the bastion use your agent while you are connected.

qs.s: You disabled password auth and reloaded sshd. ssh deploy@host now says Permission denied (publickey), but your colleague's key still works. What do you check first?
o: That your public key is in ~deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys and that ~/.ssh and the file are not group/world-writable
Whether the server's firewall blocks your IP
Whether DNS resolves the host
Whether the server's host key changed
qs.e: The server answered and offered publickey auth, so network and DNS are fine. It rejected your key: either the key is not authorized for that user, or StrictModes rejects bad permissions. ssh -v shows which keys were offered.

qs.s: Which change most reduces the risk of a successful SSH break-in on an internet-facing server?
o: Move sshd to port 2222
Install fail2ban but keep passwords enabled
Use RSA 4096 keys instead of ed25519
Disable password and keyboard-interactive auth so only keys work
qs.e: Bots guess passwords; with key-only auth there is nothing to guess. A different port cuts log noise but is found by scanners quickly. fail2ban slows guessing but does not remove it. ed25519 is already strong.

qs.s: On an Ubuntu cloud VM you add a hardening file and run sshd -t && systemctl reload ssh. Then you check the effective config. What does the last command print?

code.title: files on the server
code.src:
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config (first lines)
Include /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf

# /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/50-cloud-init.conf
PasswordAuthentication yes

# /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf
PasswordAuthentication no

$ sudo sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication

o: passwordauthentication yes: for each keyword sshd uses the first value it reads, and included files are read in name order, so 50 beats 99
passwordauthentication no: the last file wins, like most config files
Nothing: sshd -t fails because the keyword is set twice
passwordauthentication no: the main file overrides included files
qs.e: sshd_config(5): “for each keyword, the first obtained value will be used”. Name your file so it sorts first (for example 01-hardening.conf) or fix the cloud-init file, and always confirm with sshd -T. “The last file wins” is what most people expect, and it leaves password login on while you think it is off.

qs.s: You open a tunnel to reach a managed Postgres (db.internal) that only the bastion can reach. psql fails. Read the output. What is wrong?

code.title: two terminals
code.src:
# terminal 1
$ ssh -N -L 5433:localhost:5432 deploy@bastion
channel 2: open failed: connect failed: Connection refused

# terminal 2
$ psql -h localhost -p 5433 -U app orders
psql: error: connection to server at "localhost" (127.0.0.1), port 5433 failed:
  server closed the connection unexpectedly

o: Port 5433 is already used on your laptop
The bastion's firewall blocks port 5432 to the database
In -L local:host:port, the host is resolved on the bastion, so localhost means the bastion itself, where no Postgres listens. Use -L 5433:db.internal:5432
psql needs sslmode=disable over a tunnel
qs.e: The local side worked (psql connected to 5433 and SSH accepted it). The error is printed by SSH: the bastion tried to connect to its own localhost:5432 and got “refused”. A firewall drop would show a timeout, not refused. localhost is right only when the database runs on the SSH server itself.

qs.s: An engineer leaves the company. Today, 40 servers share one deploy key in authorized_keys, and everybody has a copy. What is the best long-term change?
o: Rotate the shared key on all servers every quarter

Per-person keys signed by an SSH certificate authority with short expiry (servers trust the CA via TrustedUserCAKeys), so access ends when a certificate expires and nothing has to be removed from 40 servers
Move sshd to a random high port
Store the shared key in a password manager so it cannot leak
qs.e: A shared key cannot be revoked for one person and leaves no trace of who logged in. SSH certificates (OpenSSH native; issued by tools like Vault or step-ca) give each person an identity and a short lifetime, for example 8 hours. Rotating the shared key every quarter helps, but between rotations the leaver still has access.

qs.s: Your CI deploy step looks like this. A reviewer flags the ssh line. What is the risk, and the right fix?

code.title: .github/workflows/deploy.yml (step)
code.src:
- name: Deploy
  run: |
    mkdir -p ~/.ssh
    echo "$DEPLOY_KEY" > ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
    chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
    ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no deploy@prod.example.com ./deploy.sh
  env:
    DEPLOY_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KEY }}

o: No risk: the key has mode 600
Change it to StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new, which is as safe as pinning
Switch to password auth, so no key is stored in CI

Any server that answers for that name is accepted, so a DNS hijack or man-in-the-middle receives the deploy session. Store the server's host key (fingerprint checked once out of band) in a secret and write it to ~/.ssh/known_hosts
qs.e: Host key checking is how the client knows it reached the real server. The private key is not sent, but the attacker still sees and controls everything the session sends and runs. accept-new trusts the first key it sees, and a CI runner is fresh on every run, so every run is a “first” connection: no better than no.

interview.q: How would you give 15 engineers SSH access to 200 servers, and remove it within minutes when someone leaves?
answer: One identity per person, never shared keys; FIDO2 keys (ed25519-sk) or keys with passphrases.
Option 1: config management pushes authorized_keys. Simple, but revocation depends on every server being reached.
Option 2: an SSH certificate authority issues short-lived certificates after SSO login (Vault, step-ca, Teleport). Revocation = stop issuing; old certificates expire in hours.
Option 3: no inbound SSH at all: AWS SSM Session Manager or Google IAP, with IAM-based access and full session logs.
Reach private hosts through a bastion with ProxyJump; log logins centrally; keep a tested break-glass path.
followups: How do you revoke a certificate that has not expired yet?
What are the downsides of removing SSH entirely?

interview.q: What happens when you run ssh deploy@server, from TCP to a shell prompt?
answer: TCP connection to port 22, then both sides exchange version strings and agree on algorithms.
Key exchange creates shared session keys (OpenSSH 10 defaults to the post-quantum hybrid mlkem768x25519-sha256); everything after this is encrypted.
The server proves its identity with its host key; the client checks known_hosts. This stops man-in-the-middle attacks.
User authentication: with a key, the client signs data tied to this session with the private key; the server checks the signature against authorized_keys. The private key never leaves the client.
Then channels are opened inside the one connection: the shell, commands, port forwards, agent forwarding.
followups: Why does host key checking matter if the traffic is encrypted anyway?
What exactly is the risk of agent forwarding?

interview.q: You edited sshd_config on a cloud VM and now nobody can log in. How do you recover, and how do you make sure it never happens again?
answer: Recover through a path that does not need sshd: the provider's serial console, SSM Session Manager, or stop the VM, attach its disk to a rescue VM and fix the file.
Prevent: run sshd -t before every reload, and keep one session open while testing a new login in a second terminal.
Use reload, not a full stop/start; existing sessions survive either way, but you must test a new login before closing the old one.
Manage the config with code (Ansible, cloud-init) and test it on a throwaway VM first.
Verify the effective config with sshd -T; included files and first-value-wins rules surprise people.
followups: Why does changing the port on recent Ubuntu also need a change to ssh.socket?
What would you put in a break-glass runbook?

t: Services, logs & scheduled jobs on a server
one: On a plain Linux server, systemd starts your app at boot, restarts it if it crashes, and collects its logs; cron or systemd timers run scheduled jobs.
an: A building manager who unlocks your shop every morning, reopens it if it closes unexpectedly, and keeps a diary of everything that happened.
how: A unit file (/etc/systemd/system/api.service) declares the command, user, environment and Restart=on-failure.
systemctl start|stop|restart|status api; systemctl enable api to start at boot.
journalctl -u api -f follows its logs; --since "10 min ago" filters by time.
Scheduled work: crontab -e (*/5 * * * * = every 5 minutes) or systemd timers. Cron uses the server's timezone, a common source of off-by-hours bugs.
why: Many small production apps run on one VM with Docker Compose or systemd. Knowing this lets you run and debug them without a platform team.
trade: One VM is one point of failure. Fine for small products with good backups; plan the move when uptime requirements grow.

myth.m: Running node server.js inside tmux is a deployment.
myth.r: It dies on reboot and nobody restarts it on crash. Use systemd, Docker's restart policy, or a process manager.

q.s: A cron entry 0 9 * * * was meant to run at 09:00 Tashkent time (UTC+5), but it runs at 14:00 Tashkent time. Most likely reason?
o: Cron is broken
The server's timezone is UTC, so the job runs at 09:00 UTC, which is 14:00 in Tashkent
DNS
Leap seconds
q.e: Cron uses the server's timezone. For 09:00 Tashkent on a UTC server, schedule 0 4 * * *, or use a systemd timer with an explicit timezone in OnCalendar.

lab: On a VM, write a systemd unit for a Node app running as a dedicated user with Restart=on-failure. Kill the process and watch systemd restart it.
Follow its logs with journalctl while sending requests.
Add a cron job that writes the date to a file every minute; check the timezone with timedatectl.

plain:
On a normal Linux server, you do not start your app by hand in a terminal. You give it to systemd, the system's service manager. systemd starts it when the server boots, restarts it if it crashes, and saves its logs.

For things that should run on a schedule (every night, every 5 minutes), you use cron or a systemd timer.
bridge: On Netlify or Vercel this is all done for you. On your own $5 server, systemd (or Docker with a restart policy) is the part that keeps your app alive while you sleep.

walk.title: Keeping a Node API alive on a VM
steps: Write /etc/systemd/system/api.service: the command (node /opt/api/server.js), the user to run as, environment file, and Restart=on-failure.
Run systemctl enable --now api: start it now and at every boot.
The app crashes at 3am on an uncaught error. systemd notices and restarts it within seconds.
In the morning you run journalctl -u api --since "03:00" and see the crash stack trace right before the restart.
You fix the bug, deploy, and systemctl restart api.

terms: The program that starts and supervises services on most Linux servers.
A config file describing one service.
The command to read logs collected by systemd.
The classic scheduler; */5 * * * * means every 5 minutes.
insights: Keep servers on UTC. Convert to local time in the app. Timezone bugs in cron are extremely common.
systemctl status api shows the state, the last exit code and the last 10 log lines. Read it before anything else.
After editing a unit file, run systemctl daemon-reload. Otherwise systemd keeps using the old version and your change seems to do nothing.

prod.summary: On a VM, systemd is your orchestrator: it starts the app at boot, restarts it on crash, limits its resources and collects its logs. Seniors write unit files that run as a dedicated user, restart with a delay, survive reboots, and send logs somewhere that will not fill the disk.
checklist: The unit runs as a dedicated user (User=api), never root, and reads secrets from an EnvironmentFile= with mode 600.
Restart=on-failure (or always) with RestartSec= a few seconds, so a crash loop does not hammer the database.
systemctl enable was run, and the server was actually rebooted once to prove the app comes back.
LimitNOFILE= is raised for network services; the default soft limit of 1024 open files is low for a busy API.
Journald storage is persistent (/var/log/journal exists) so logs survive a reboot, and its size cap is known.
Scheduled jobs use systemd timers with Persistent=true (runs missed jobs after downtime), or cron with output redirected to a log, plus an alert when the job does not run.
numbers: systemd DefaultRestartSec is 100 ms; with the default start limit (5 starts in 10 s) a crash-looping service is given up as failed within seconds.
systemd DefaultTimeoutStopSec is 90 s before SIGKILL.
journald SystemMaxUse defaults to 10% of the filesystem, capped at 4 GB; with Storage=auto logs are lost on reboot unless /var/log/journal exists.
Cron's smallest interval is 1 minute; systemd timers can go lower and add RandomizedDelaySec= to avoid every server firing at once.
failures: systemctl status api shows failed (Result: start-limit-hit) and the app stays down.
It crashed 5 times in 10 s and systemd stopped retrying. Fix the crash (read journalctl -u api -n 100), set RestartSec=5, then systemctl reset-failed api && systemctl start api.
The app works when started by hand but the unit fails with node: not found or a missing env var.
systemd does not load your shell profile, nvm or .bashrc. Use absolute paths in ExecStart= (/usr/bin/node) and put variables in Environment= or EnvironmentFile=.
A nightly backup cron job silently stopped working weeks ago.
Cron output goes to local mail nobody reads. Log to a file or journald, and use a dead-man's-switch alert (a ping URL that alerts when the job does not report in).
After a reboot, journalctl -u api has no history from before the crash.
Journal storage was volatile (in RAM). Create /var/log/journal or set Storage=persistent in journald.conf.

code.title: systemd service and timer for a Node API
code.src:
# /etc/systemd/system/api.service
[Unit]
Description=Orders API
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=api
WorkingDirectory=/opt/api
EnvironmentFile=/etc/api/env
ExecStart=/usr/bin/node server.js
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
TimeoutStopSec=30
LimitNOFILE=65536
NoNewPrivileges=true

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

# /etc/systemd/system/cleanup.timer  (runs cleanup.service)
[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 04:00:00 UTC
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

# sudo systemctl daemon-reload
# sudo systemctl enable --now api cleanup.timer
code.note: TimeoutStopSec=30 gives the app 30 s after SIGTERM to drain. Persistent=true runs the 04:00 job at boot if the server was off at 04:00. Check timers with systemctl list-timers.

qs.s: You edited api.service to add a new environment variable and ran systemctl restart api. The app still does not see the variable. What did you forget?
o: systemctl enable api
journalctl --rotate
Rebooting the server
systemctl daemon-reload, so systemd re-reads the changed unit file
qs.e: systemd caches unit files. After editing one, daemon-reload is required; systemd usually warns “unit file changed on disk”. enable only affects boot.

qs.s: A crash-looping service shows start-limit-hit. The unit has Restart=always and no RestartSec. Why did systemd stop restarting it?
o: Restart=always has a hidden maximum of 3 restarts
With the 100 ms default delay it hit the start limit (5 starts in 10 s) and systemd marked it failed
The OOM killer disabled the unit
systemd never restarts units that exit with code 1
qs.e: The restart delay defaults to 100 ms, so 5 restarts happen within 10 s, which trips StartLimitBurst/StartLimitIntervalSec. A RestartSec=5 spaces restarts out and gives dependencies time to recover.

qs.s: A cleanup job must run daily. The VM is sometimes stopped overnight to save money. Which setup makes sure the job still runs?
o: A systemd timer with OnCalendar=daily and Persistent=true
A cron entry 0 3 * * *
A cron entry @reboot only
A while true; sleep 86400 loop in tmux
qs.e: Persistent=true records the last run and fires a missed run at the next boot. Classic cron simply skips runs that happen while the machine is off. @reboot runs on every boot, not daily.

qs.s: Node was installed with nvm in /home/deploy/.nvm. node /opt/api/server.js works in your shell, but the service fails. Read the unit and the log. What is the cause?

code.title: api.service + journal
code.src:
[Service]
User=api
ExecStart=node /opt/api/server.js
Environment=NODE_ENV=production
Restart=always

$ journalctl -u api -n 3
api.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=203/EXEC
api.service: Failed with result 'exit-code'.

o: User api cannot read server.js
NODE_ENV=production must be in quotes

systemd could not execute node: it does not load your shell profile, so the nvm path is unknown (and api cannot use another user's nvm anyway). Install Node system-wide and use an absolute path like /usr/bin/node
Restart=always hides the real error code
qs.e: Status 203/EXEC means the execve() of the command itself failed, before Node ran any code. If Node had started and failed to read server.js, you would see Node's own error and exit status 1. systemd searches only a fixed list of system directories for a bare command name, never ~/.nvm.

qs.s: The API and Postgres run on the same VM. After every reboot, the API logs ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432 once, then works after a restart. What is wrong in the unit?

code.title: api.service (excerpt)
code.src:
[Unit]
Description=Orders API
Requires=postgresql.service

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/node /opt/api/server.js
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5

o: Requires= only says “start Postgres too”, not “start it first”. Add After=postgresql.service for ordering, and let the app retry its first DB connection
Requires= should be Wants=
RestartSec=5 is too short
Postgres must be started from the API's ExecStartPre=
qs.e: In systemd, requirement and ordering are separate. Without After=, both start in parallel, and the API can try to connect before Postgres listens. Even with After=, “started” is not always “ready”, so retry logic in the app is still wise. Wants= only makes the dependency weaker; it does not add order.

qs.s: A cron job */5 * * * * /opt/sync.sh usually takes 2 minutes, but sometimes 8. On those days two copies run at once and write duplicate rows. Which fix is right?
o: Change the schedule to */10
Run the script with nice so it finishes faster
Add Restart=always
Wrap it in flock -n /run/sync.lock /opt/sync.sh, or move it to a systemd timer, which does not start a service that is still running
qs.e: Cron does not know or care whether the last run finished. flock -n makes the second copy exit immediately if the lock is held. A timer triggers a oneshot service; starting a unit that is already active does nothing. A longer interval such as */10 only makes overlaps rarer: a 12-minute run still overlaps.

qs.s: The API restarts a few times a day. Read the unit and the journal. What is happening?

code.title: api.service + journal
code.src:
[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/node --max-old-space-size=4096 /opt/api/server.js
MemoryMax=2G
Restart=on-failure

$ journalctl -u api --since today | tail -3
api.service: A process of this unit has been killed by the OOM killer.
api.service: Main process exited, code=killed, status=9/KILL
api.service: Failed with result 'oom-kill'.

o: The whole server ran out of RAM; add swap
The unit's own cgroup limit (MemoryMax=2G) was hit. V8 was told it may use a 4 GB heap, so it does not collect hard enough before 2 GB. Set --max-old-space-size to about 1.5 GB, or raise MemoryMax
journald killed the process for logging too much
systemd kills services at 95% of their memory by default
qs.e: MemoryMax= is a hard cgroup limit: going above it triggers the OOM killer inside that cgroup, even if the host has free memory. The heap flag must leave room under the limit for the rest of Node's memory (buffers, native code). “The whole server ran out of RAM” is the usual guess, but the log says the kill was for this unit, and the host may be fine.

interview.q: You must run a Node API on one VM without Docker. Walk me through a production-ready setup.
answer: A dedicated system user, code in /opt/api, Node installed system-wide, absolute paths in ExecStart=.
A unit with Restart=on-failure, RestartSec=, secrets in an EnvironmentFile= with mode 600, LimitNOFILE=, TimeoutStopSec= matched to the app's graceful shutdown, MemoryMax=.
Hardening options: NoNewPrivileges=true, ProtectSystem=strict + ReadWritePaths=, PrivateTmp=true; systemd-analyze security api scores the unit.
nginx or Caddy terminates TLS on 443; the app listens on 127.0.0.1:3000.
Deploy into a new release directory, switch a symlink, restart, run a health check, keep the previous release for rollback.
Persistent journald plus log shipping, an uptime check, backups, and one real reboot test.
followups: How do you get zero-downtime restarts with only one process?
What would make you move this to containers?

interview.q: cron or systemd timers: when do you pick each?
answer: cron: simple and everywhere; runs in the server's timezone; output goes to local mail unless redirected; no overlap protection; missed runs are skipped.
Timers: logs in the journal, Persistent=true runs missed jobs after downtime, RandomizedDelaySec= spreads load, no overlapping runs, resource limits and dependencies from the service unit.
Timers can set a timezone in OnCalendar=; check the schedule with systemctl list-timers and systemd-analyze calendar.
On Kubernetes, use a CronJob with concurrencyPolicy: Forbid and startingDeadlineSeconds.
Whatever the tool, add a dead-man's-switch alert: you want to know when a job did not run.
followups: How do you make a scheduled job safe if it runs twice?
How would you schedule 09:00 Tashkent time on a UTC server?

interview.q: A service restarts several times every night. How do you investigate?
answer: systemctl status api: the Result (exit-code, signal, oom-kill, start-limit-hit) already narrows the cause; systemctl show -p NRestarts api counts restarts.
journalctl -u api --since "02:00" --until "04:00" for the app's last lines; -b -1 for the previous boot.
Read the exit status: 203/EXEC = could not start; 1 = app error; 9/KILL with oom-kill = memory; check journalctl -k for kernel OOM messages.
Look at what else runs at night: backups, logrotate, timers and cron (systemctl list-timers) can cause memory, disk or CPU pressure.
Fix the cause, then check that restart settings (RestartSec, start limits) would not hide the next problem.
followups: Where do core dumps go, and how do you read one?
How do you alert on restarts, not just on downtime?
