one: A handful of commands answer "is it DNS, the network, the port, TLS, or the app?" in a minute.
an: A plumber's toolkit: check the street supply, the pipe to the house, the valve, then the tap, in that order.
how: DNS: dig api.example.com. Reachability: ping, path: traceroute/mtr.
Port open? nc -vz host 5432. Who is listening locally? lsof -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN (macOS) or ss -ltnp (Linux).
HTTP and TLS: curl -v shows DNS, connect, TLS handshake, request and response headers. curl -w times each phase.
Inside containers, tools are often missing; docker run --rm -it --network container:<id> nicolaka/netshoot gives you all of them in the same network namespace.
why: "It doesn't connect" is a daily problem. Narrowing the layer quickly is a senior habit.
trade: Firewalls often drop ping (ICMP), so a failed ping alone does not prove a host is down.

myth.m: If ping works, the service works.
myth.r: Ping proves the host answers ICMP. The port, TLS and app can each still be broken.

q.s: curl https://api.example.com hangs, but dig returns the right IP. What do you check next?
o: Change DNS provider
Whether the port is reachable (nc -vz host 443) and where it stops in curl -v
Rebuild the frontend
Clear browser cache
q.e: DNS is fine, so move down a layer: TCP connect, then TLS, then the app.

lab: Break things on purpose and diagnose with the tools: stop a local server (connection refused), firewall a port (timeout), put a wrong IP in /etc/hosts (wrong host), use an expired-cert test site like expired.badssl.com (TLS error). Note each error's exact text.
docs: Julia Evans: Networking zines and tools

plain: When something “cannot connect”, the problem is in one of a few layers: the name lookup (DNS), the network path, the port, the encryption (TLS), or the app itself. A few terminal commands check each layer in order, so you stop guessing.
bridge: The DevTools Network tab shows you the same layers for browser requests: the Timing tab splits DNS, connection, TLS and waiting time. The terminal tools do that for servers and containers, where there is no DevTools.

walk.title: “The API is down” — narrowing it down in 2 minutes
steps: dig api.example.com — DNS returns an IP. DNS is fine.
nc -vz api.example.com 443 — “succeeded”. The network and port are fine.
curl -v https://api.example.com/health — TLS handshake works, but the server answers 502 Bad Gateway.
502 means the proxy is fine but the app behind it is not answering. So the problem is the app, not the network.
You check the app logs and find it crashed after the last deploy. Total time: two minutes, no guessing.

terms: Shows DNS answers for a name.
Tests whether a port accepts connections.
Makes an HTTP request and prints every step.
Refused: the machine said no (nothing listening). Timeout: no answer (firewall or wrong host).
insights: Error messages tell you the layer: “could not resolve host” = DNS, “connection refused” = port, “certificate” = TLS, 5xx = app.
Check from the same place the failing code runs (inside the container), not from your laptop.
curl -v prints * Trying 10.0.4.7:443...: the IP it really used. Compare it with the IP you expect; a stale DNS record or an old /etc/hosts line shows up right there.

prod.summary: In production, “it cannot connect” is solved by checking one layer at a time, from the place where the failing code runs (inside the pod or container, not your laptop). Seniors read the exact error text: it almost always names the layer — DNS, TCP, TLS or the app.
checklist: Reproduce from the same network as the failing code: kubectl exec, kubectl debug with a netshoot image, or docker run --network container:<id> nicolaka/netshoot.
DNS: dig +short name from inside, and compare with what you expected; check /etc/resolv.conf and /etc/hosts.
TCP: nc -vz host port. “Refused” = host reachable, nothing listening; “timed out” = firewall, security group or wrong IP.
Listening side: ss -ltnp on the server shows whether the app binds 127.0.0.1 (local only) or 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces).
TLS: openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host shows the certificate chain, expiry and SNI problems.
HTTP: curl -v for headers and status, curl -w for per-phase timings; check proxy variables (HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY).
numbers: Linux default net.ipv4.tcp_syn_retries is 6, so a connect to a host that silently drops packets takes about 2 minutes to fail (127–131 s depending on kernel version) unless the client sets its own timeout.
curl exit codes name the layer: 6 = could not resolve host, 7 = failed to connect, 28 = timeout, 60 = certificate problem.
nginx returns 502 when the upstream refuses or breaks the connection, and 504 when the upstream does not answer within proxy_read_timeout (default 60 s).
failures: curl: (7) Failed to connect to localhost port 3000: Connection refused from another container, though the app is running.
Inside a container, localhost is that container itself. Use the service name (http://api:3000) and make sure the app listens on 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1.
Requests hang about 2 minutes, then fail with ETIMEDOUT.

Packets are silently dropped (security group, firewall, wrong subnet route), and the client has no connect timeout, so it waits for the kernel's SYN retries. Fix the rule; also set explicit connect timeouts in clients.
Browser works, but server-side calls fail: unable to get local issuer certificate / UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE.
The server sends only its leaf certificate without the intermediate. Browsers often fetch the missing intermediate; Node and curl do not. Serve the full chain (fullchain.pem).
Works in staging, intermittent EAI_AGAIN / getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND in production under load.

DNS lookups are failing or being throttled (for example, CoreDNS overloaded or conntrack issues). Check DNS server metrics, cache lookups in the app, and use a fully qualified name with a trailing dot to cut search-domain queries in Kubernetes.

code.title: Find which layer is slow or broken
code.src:
# 1. DNS
dig +short api.example.com

# 2. TCP port
nc -vz -w 3 api.example.com 443

# 3. TLS: chain, expiry, SNI
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com </dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -enddate

# 4. HTTP with per-phase timing (seconds since start)
curl -sS -o /dev/null --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 15 \
  -w 'dns=%{time_namelookup} tcp=%{time_connect} tls=%{time_appconnect} ttfb=%{time_starttransfer} total=%{time_total} code=%{http_code}\n' \
  https://api.example.com/health

# 5. On the server: who listens where?
sudo ss -ltnp | grep ':3000'
code.note: The timings are cumulative. If tls is 0.05 and ttfb is 2.9, the network is fine and the app spends almost 3 s before the first byte.

qs.s: curl -w prints dns=0.004 tcp=0.020 tls=0.061 ttfb=3.410 total=3.415. Users say the endpoint is slow. Where do you look?
o: The application or its dependencies: about 3.35 s pass between the TLS handshake finishing and the first response byte
DNS: switch to a faster resolver
The network path: run traceroute
TLS: the handshake is too slow
qs.e: Timings are cumulative. DNS, TCP and TLS together take 61 ms. The gap until the first byte is server think time: slow queries, external calls, locks.

qs.s: On the server, ss -ltnp shows LISTEN 127.0.0.1:8080 users:(("node",pid=812)). From another machine, nc -vz server 8080 says “Connection refused”. Most likely cause?
o: The firewall drops the packets
DNS points to the wrong server
The app is overloaded
The app binds only to the loopback interface, so nothing listens on the public IP's port 8080
qs.e: Bound to 127.0.0.1, it only accepts local connections; the kernel answers others with a reset (refused). A firewall drop would show a timeout, not refused. Bind to 0.0.0.0 (or the private IP) and control access with the firewall.

qs.s: A Node service calling a partner API sometimes hangs for about 2 minutes before ETIMEDOUT, while the partner says their API is up. What is the best first change on your side?
o: Retry immediately 10 times
Set an explicit connect and request timeout (for example AbortSignal.timeout(5000)) and check if some resolved IPs are unreachable from your network
Increase tcp_syn_retries
Switch from HTTPS to HTTP
qs.e: About 2 minutes matches the kernel's default SYN retries: packets to some address are dropped. A short timeout turns a hung worker into a fast, retryable error, and checking each resolved IP (for example IPv6 vs IPv4) finds the unreachable one.

qs.s: A service calls an internal API and fails. Read the curl -v output. Which layer is broken, and what is the correct fix?

code.title: curl -v https://api.internal/health
code.src:
* Host api.internal:443 was resolved.
* IPv4: 10.0.3.25
*   Trying 10.0.3.25:443...
* Connected to api.internal (10.0.3.25) port 443
* ALPN: curl offers h2,http/1.1
* TLSv1.3 (OUT), TLS handshake, Client hello (1):
* TLSv1.3 (IN), TLS handshake, Server hello (2):
* SSL: no alternative certificate subject name matches target host name 'api.internal'
curl: (60) SSL: no alternative certificate subject name matches target host name 'api.internal'

o: DNS: the name resolves to the wrong IP
TCP: port 443 is blocked
TLS, and the fix is curl -k (or NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 in the service)
TLS: the certificate does not list api.internal in its Subject Alternative Names. Issue a certificate that includes that name, or call the service by a name the certificate has
qs.e: DNS resolved and TCP connected, so the problem starts at the TLS handshake. Exit code 60 is a certificate verification failure. Turning verification off (curl -k, NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0) makes the error go away and also removes the protection against man-in-the-middle attacks; it must never ship.

qs.s: From the app server, Postgres is unreachable. Read both outputs. What is the most likely cause?

code.title: two servers
code.src:
# on the app server
$ nc -vz -w 5 10.0.1.5 5432
nc: connect to 10.0.1.5 port 5432 (tcp) timed out: Operation now in progress

# on the database server
$ sudo ss -ltnp | grep 5432
LISTEN 0  200  0.0.0.0:5432  0.0.0.0:*  users:(("postgres",pid=901,fd=6))

o: Postgres is down
A firewall or security group silently drops the packets; check the inbound rule on the DB for the app server's source address
listen_addresses is set to localhost
pg_hba.conf rejects the app server
qs.e: Postgres listens on all interfaces, so a listen_addresses problem and a stopped Postgres are ruled out by ss. A timeout means no answer at all: something drops the SYN. If nothing listened, you would get “refused” at once. pg_hba.conf works after the TCP connection is made, and it gives an authentication error, not a timeout.

qs.s: A pod calls api.stripe.com. Read its /etc/resolv.conf. Which name does the resolver try first?

code.title: /etc/resolv.conf in the pod
code.src:
search default.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
nameserver 10.96.0.10
options ndots:5

o: api.stripe.com.default.svc.cluster.local, because the name has fewer than 5 dots, so the search domains are tried before the name itself
api.stripe.com, because it is a public domain
api.stripe.com.cluster.local
Only api.stripe.com; search domains apply to short names without dots
qs.e: With ndots:5, any name with fewer than 5 dots is tried with each search domain first: three failed lookups (each often for A and AAAA) before the real one. Under load this multiplies DNS traffic. Write the name with a trailing dot (api.stripe.com.) or lower ndots in the pod's dnsConfig. “Search domains apply only to short names without dots” is how many people think search domains work.

qs.s: After the platform team added a corporate proxy, curl http://orders.internal:8080/health from a container returns 403 Forbidden with the header Server: squid. env shows http_proxy=http://proxy.corp:3128. What is going on?
o: The orders service has a new authentication bug
DNS now resolves orders.internal to the proxy
curl reads http_proxy and sends the request to the proxy, which refuses internal hosts. Add orders.internal (or .internal) to no_proxy
Port 8080 is blocked by the firewall
qs.e: The Server: squid header shows the answer came from the proxy, not from your service. Many tools (curl, Python requests, Go's default client) honour the proxy variables; internal names must be excluded with no_proxy/NO_PROXY. A firewall block would give a timeout or refused, not an HTTP 403.

interview.q: Service A in Kubernetes cannot reach service B. Walk me through your debugging.
answer: Read the exact error first; it usually names the layer (DNS, refused, timeout, TLS, HTTP status).
Reproduce from A's network: kubectl debug or an ephemeral netshoot container, not from your laptop.
DNS: dig b.namespace.svc.cluster.local; if it fails, look at CoreDNS.
Does the Service have endpoints? kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=b. Empty means the selector does not match or no pod is Ready.
Check port vs targetPort, then connect straight to a pod IP to skip the Service; check that the app binds 0.0.0.0.
If pod IP works from some places but not others: NetworkPolicy, or a mesh/sidecar policy.
followups: What does it mean if the pod IP works but the Service IP does not?
How does a NetworkPolicy block show up: refused or timeout?

interview.q: Explain “connection refused”, “connection timed out” and “connection reset”. What does each one tell you?
answer: Refused: the host answered the SYN with a RST. The machine is reachable, but nothing listens on that port (or the app binds only 127.0.0.1, or a firewall uses REJECT).

Timed out: no answer at all. A firewall or security group drops packets, the route is wrong, or the host is down. With Linux defaults a connect waits about 2 minutes, so clients need their own connect timeout.
Reset: an established connection was torn down by the other side or by something in between: an app crash, a proxy limit, or an idle timeout on a load balancer or NAT.

Classic reset bug: a client reuses a keep-alive socket the server has just closed. Node's default keepAliveTimeout is 5 s; behind an AWS ALB (60 s idle timeout) set the server timeout higher than the load balancer's.
Use nc -vz, ss and, for resets, tcpdump to see who sends the RST.
followups: Why should the server keep-alive timeout be longer than the load balancer's?
How would you capture the RST with tcpdump?

interview.q: Users in one region say the API is slow; your dashboards look fine. How do you find where the time goes?
answer: Measure from that region: curl -w timings for DNS, TCP, TLS and time to first byte, from a VM or a synthetic check there.
Network cost is round trips × latency: a new HTTPS connection needs TCP + TLS round trips before the request. Connection reuse, TLS 1.3 and HTTP/2 cut them.
Check for packet loss on the path with mtr; a small loss rate causes large tail latency through retransmits.
Compare client-side numbers with server-side traces: if the server spends 50 ms and the user waits 900 ms, the time is in the network, DNS or the CDN.
Look at real-user monitoring split by region, and whether a CDN or a closer region would help.
followups: Why can p99 be bad while the average looks fine?
When would you add a region instead of a CDN?

t: CPU, memory & disk on a server
one: Reading load, memory and disk usage tells you whether a slow or crashing server is starved of CPU, memory, disk space or I/O.
an: A delivery van: is the engine maxed out (CPU), is the cargo area full (memory), is the trailer full (disk), or is the loading dock jammed (I/O)?
how: top/htop: per-process CPU and memory. Load average on Linux counts processes that are running or waiting for CPU and those blocked on disk I/O (state D); compare it with the number of cores, and check %wa (I/O wait) before blaming the CPU.

free -h: memory. The number to watch is “available” (free memory plus cache the kernel can drop), not “free”. When memory runs out, the OOM killer kills the process with the highest oom_score (mostly its memory use, adjusted by oom_score_adj). Evidence: dmesg or journalctl -k | grep -i oom.
df -h: disk space per filesystem; df -i: inodes (file count); du -sh * | sort -h: what is using it. Full disks break databases and logs in confusing ways.
Containers are limited by cgroups, but free and top inside them often show the host's totals. Check docker stats, kubectl top pod, or /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max and memory.current.
why: "Server is slow" incidents are often full disks, swap thrashing or an OOM-killed process. These commands find that in minutes.
trade: Swap prevents crashes but makes everything crawl; many container setups disable it.

myth.m: Linux is using 95% of RAM, we need more memory.
myth.r: Linux uses free RAM as disk cache and gives it back on demand. Check "available", not "used".

q.s: Postgres suddenly errors with "could not write to file" and the app logs stopped. First command?
o: top
df -h to check disk space
ping
dig
q.e: Both symptoms point to a full disk, often from logs or WAL growth.

lab: Fill a disk on a test VM with fallocate -l 5G big.file and watch which services fail and how.
Run a memory-hungry script in a container with --memory=100m and find the OOM evidence afterwards.
Read htop on a busy machine and explain each column at the top.

plain:
A server has limited CPU, memory and disk. When a server is slow or crashing, one of these is usually exhausted. A few commands show which one.

CPU full = everything is slow. Memory full = programs get killed. Disk full = writes fail, often with strange errors from databases and logs.
bridge: This is the server version of Chrome's Task Manager (Shift+Esc), which shows which tab is eating CPU and memory.

walk.title: The site is broken and the logs stopped
steps: Users report errors. Strangely, the app logs stopped an hour ago.
df -h shows the main disk at 100%.
du -sh /var/log/* | sort -h finds a 40 GB debug log file that was never rotated.
You run rm on it, but df still says 100%: the app still has the file open, so the kernel keeps the space. lsof +L1 lists such deleted-but-open files.
The right move is truncate -s 0 on the file (or restart the process holding it). Space returns, the database and app recover, and you add log rotation plus an alert on disk above 80%.

terms: Average number of processes running, waiting for CPU, or stuck waiting for disk, over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. Compare with the number of cores.
The kernel feature that kills the process with the highest OOM score when memory runs out.
Disk used as emergency memory. Prevents crashes but is very slow.
Disk free (per disk) / disk usage (per folder).
CPU time spent idle while waiting for disk. High values mean the disk, not the CPU, is the bottleneck.
insights: Alert on the trend, not only the level: a disk at 70% that grows 5% a day is a full disk in six days.
Full disks cause the most confusing outages because every symptom looks different. Check df -h early.
In containers, limits come from cgroups. The container may be killed while the host still has plenty of memory.

prod.summary: In production, most “server is slow” or “app keeps restarting” incidents come down to one exhausted resource: CPU, memory, disk space, inodes, disk I/O or file descriptors. Seniors use the USE method (Utilization, Saturation, Errors per resource), alert before the limit, and know that containers see their limits through cgroups, not through free.
checklist: Alerts exist for disk above 80–85%, inode use, memory “available” trending down, and containers restarting with OOMKilled.
Logs are rotated (logrotate, Docker max-size, journald caps); Docker's default json-file log driver has no size limit.
Every container has a memory limit, and the runtime heap fits inside it (Node: --max-old-space-size below the limit, leaving room for native memory).
CPU limits are checked for throttling (container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total); a pod can be slow at 50% average CPU because it is throttled in bursts.
ulimit -n / LimitNOFILE is high enough for the connection count; the common soft default is 1024.
Postgres or other databases live on a disk with headroom for WAL and temporary files, not on the same full root disk as the logs.
numbers: Container exit code 137 with Kubernetes reason OOMKilled = the cgroup memory limit was hit.
oom_score_adj ranges from -1000 (never kill) to 1000 (kill first).
ext4 reserves 5% of blocks for root by default, so a normal user can hit “No space left” while df shows a few percent free.
Load average 8 on a 4-core machine means roughly twice as much demand as capacity — if the processes are in R state; in D state it means a disk bottleneck.
failures: Pod restarts every few hours; kubectl describe pod shows Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137.

The container hit its memory limit: a leak or a heap allowed to grow past the limit. Compare memory over time; set --max-old-space-size to about 75% of the limit and find the leak with a heap snapshot.
No space left on device, but df -h shows 40% free.
Inodes are exhausted (millions of small files: sessions, cache). df -i confirms. Delete the files and fix whatever creates them.
df shows the disk full, du adds up to much less, and deleting logs did not help.
Deleted files still held open by a process. lsof +L1 lists them; restart or signal the process to reopen logs, and next time truncate instead of rm.
Error: EMFILE: too many open files under load.
The process hit its file descriptor limit (each socket is one). Raise LimitNOFILE in the unit or ulimit -n, and check for leaked connections that are never closed.
Load average 20 on an 8-core box, but CPU is 70% idle and the app is slow.
Processes are blocked on disk (D state; high %wa). Check iostat -x 1 for a saturated device and find the heavy writer with iotop or pidstat -d.

code.title: First 60 seconds on a slow server
code.src:
uptime                      # load averages vs core count (nproc)
nproc
dmesg -T | tail -20         # OOM kills, disk errors
vmstat 1 5                  # r = run queue, wa = I/O wait, si/so = swapping
free -h                     # look at "available"
df -h; df -i                # space and inodes
iostat -x 1 3               # %util and await per disk (sysstat)
pidstat 1 3                 # which process uses CPU
sudo lsof +L1               # deleted files still holding space

# inside a container / cgroup v2
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.current
code.note: Based on Brendan Gregg's “Linux performance analysis in 60 seconds”. vmstat separates CPU pressure (high r) from disk pressure (high wa) in one screen.

qs.s: A 4-core VM shows load average 12.0. vmstat 1 shows r around 1, wa at 60%, and us+sy under 15%. What is the bottleneck?
o: CPU: add more cores
Memory: the server is swapping
Network bandwidth
Disk I/O: most of the load is processes waiting on disk (D state)
qs.e: Linux load includes uninterruptible disk waits. Only ~1 process wants CPU, and 60% of time is I/O wait. More cores would not help; find the device and process doing the I/O.

qs.s: A Node container has a 512 MiB memory limit. Inside it, free -h shows 15 GiB available, yet the container is OOMKilled at about 500 MiB. Why?
o: free is broken in Alpine
Node's default heap is always 512 MiB
free reads the host's /proc/meminfo; the cgroup limit (512 MiB) is what the kernel enforces
The host ran out of memory
qs.e: Classic tools read host-wide numbers. The cgroup limit is in /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max. Size Node's heap well below the limit so native memory and buffers fit too.

qs.s: A box's root disk is 100% full. You find a 30 GB app.log being written by the running API. Which action frees space immediately without dropping traffic?
o: rm app.log
truncate -s 0 app.log (or : > app.log), then add rotation
mv app.log /tmp/ on the same disk
chmod 000 app.log
qs.e: rm only removes the name; the open file keeps its blocks until the process closes it. Truncating frees the space in place while the process keeps writing. Moving on the same filesystem frees nothing.

qs.s: The app is slow. Read the output. What is the right conclusion?

code.title: free -h ; vmstat 1
code.src:
total   used   free  shared  buff/cache  available
Mem:            15Gi   13Gi  320Mi   1.1Gi       2.1Gi      1.4Gi
Swap:          2.0Gi  1.9Gi  100Mi

procs ---------memory-------- ---swap-- ---io----
 r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so   bi   bo
 3  4 1990000 320000  1200 2100000  850 1200  900 1400

o: Real memory pressure: only 1.4 GiB available, swap almost full and pages moving in and out of swap every second (si/so). Find the process with the largest RSS and fix or limit it
Nothing is wrong: Linux uses free RAM as cache, so a high “used” is normal
The disk is the bottleneck; memory is fine
Run echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches to free memory
qs.e: “Look at available, not used” is right, and here available is low too. Active swapping (non-zero si/so every second) makes everything slow. “Nothing is wrong, it is only cache” applies the right rule to the wrong numbers. Dropping caches frees a little cache and makes the disk work harder; it does not fix the process using the memory.

qs.s: A container has this CPU limit. One request needs 120 ms of CPU time on one thread, and nothing else runs. About how long does it take, at best?

code.title: deployment.yaml (excerpt)
code.src:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 500m
  limits:
    cpu: 500m      # CFS quota: 50 ms of CPU per 100 ms period

o: 120 ms
240 ms
About 220 ms: 50 ms runs in period 1, 50 ms in period 2, the last 20 ms early in period 3
It never finishes, because 120 ms is more than the 50 ms quota
qs.e: The quota is refilled every 100 ms period. After using 50 ms the container is throttled until the next period. 100 + 100 + 20 = about 220 ms. “240 ms” treats it as a simple half-speed CPU. In real apps it is often worse: GC and libuv threads use the same quota in parallel. That is why latency-sensitive services watch the throttling metrics.

qs.s: Disk on a Docker host is 100% full. Read the output. Which /etc/docker/daemon.json change prevents this for new containers?

code.title: terminal
code.src:
$ sudo du -sh /var/lib/docker/containers/*/*-json.log | sort -h | tail -2
1.2G  /var/lib/docker/containers/9f1c.../9f1c...-json.log
38G   /var/lib/docker/containers/a73e.../a73e...-json.log
$ docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.LogConfig}}' a73e
{json-file map[]}

o: {"log-driver": "none"}
{"log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"}}, then recreate the containers
{"log-opts": {"max-size": 10}}
{"storage-driver": "overlay2"}
qs.e: The default json-file driver has no size limit (map[] = no options). The json-file answer with max-size and max-file caps each container at about 30 MB of logs. It applies only to containers created after the daemon restart. "max-size": 10 is invalid: log-opts values in daemon.json must be strings, and a size needs a unit. "log-driver": "none" stops the disk filling but throws away all logs.

qs.s: Writes are slow on a database server. Read the output. What does it show?

code.title: iostat -x 1
code.src:
Device   r/s     w/s   rkB/s     wkB/s  r_await  w_await  aqu-sz  %util
nvme0n1  12.0  4200.0   96.0  168000.0     0.4     38.5   161.7  100.0

o: %util is 100%, so the disk is at its limit and must be replaced; nothing else in the output matters
Reads are the problem
The network is saturated
Writes are queuing: about 4,200 writes/s waiting 38 ms each, with ~160 requests in the queue, on a device that normally answers in under a millisecond. Find the writer with pidstat -d 1 or iotop
qs.e: Read the wait time (w_await) and queue size (aqu-sz): they show saturation. On SSDs and NVMe, %util only means “busy at least once in each sample”; these devices serve many requests in parallel, so 100% does not always mean full. Here the high await confirms it. Reads wait only 0.4 ms.

interview.q: You SSH into a slow Linux server. You have five minutes. What do you run, and what are you looking for?
answer: Use the USE method: for each resource, check Utilization, Saturation and Errors.
uptime (load vs nproc), dmesg -T | tail (OOM kills, disk errors), vmstat 1 (run queue r, blocked b, wa, swap si/so).
mpstat -P ALL 1 for one hot core, pidstat 1 for the process using CPU, iostat -x 1 for disk await and queue, free -h, df -h / df -i.
sar -n DEV 1 or ss -s for network and socket counts; /proc/pressure/* (PSI) shows how long tasks waited for CPU, memory or I/O.
Write down what you found before you change anything, and compare with what is normal for that box.
followups: Load is high but CPU is idle. What next?
How does this change inside a container?

interview.q: How do memory limits work for containers, and what happens when one is hit?
answer: Limits are cgroup v2 settings: memory.max is the hard limit; memory.high slows the group down and reclaims memory before that.
Above memory.max, the kernel OOM killer runs inside that cgroup: the container exits with 137 and Kubernetes shows OOMKilled, even if the node has free memory.
Page cache is counted too, but the kernel can reclaim clean cache first; anonymous memory (heap) is what usually causes the kill.
Kubernetes: requests drive scheduling, limits drive kills; QoS classes decide which pods are evicted first when the node itself is short.
Runtimes must fit inside: Node --max-old-space-size, JVM -XX:MaxRAMPercentage, leaving room for native memory.
followups: Why can kubectl top show more memory than the app's heap?
Requests equal to limits: what do you gain and lose?

interview.q: Should you set CPU limits on Kubernetes workloads?
answer: Requests decide scheduling and the CPU share under contention; set them for every pod.
Limits become a CFS quota: the container is throttled after its quota in each 100 ms period, even when the node has idle CPU. This shows up as latency spikes at low average CPU.
Many teams set requests only for latency-sensitive services and keep limits for batch jobs, noisy tenants, or when Guaranteed QoS is required.
If you keep limits, watch the ratio of container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total to container_cpu_cfs_periods_total.
Match thread counts to the quota: many runtimes size thread pools from the host's core count unless told otherwise (Go became container-aware in 1.25).
followups: A pod at 30% average CPU has bad p99. How do you prove it is throttling?
How do requests and limits affect QoS class and eviction?

diagrams.title: Why rm did not free the disk
diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant Y as You
  participant A as App (file open)
  participant F as Filesystem
  A->>F: open debug.log, keep writing
  Note over F: disk 100%, 40 GB in debug.log
  Y->>F: rm debug.log
  F-->>Y: name removed
  Note over F: data stays, the app still holds it open
  Y->>F: df -h

    A->>F: process exits, file closed
    F-->>Y: space freed

diagrams.caption: What to notice: rm only removes the name. Space comes back when the last open handle closes. lsof +L1 lists deleted files that are still open.
